performers: Roxana Pavel Goldstein, violin; Constance Schoepflin, flute; Matthew Ganong, harpsichord; Advent Chamber Orchestra
intro: The orchestra sits out, leaving flute, violin and harpsichord to themselves. Their dotted phrases answer one another in B minor, with the keyboard slipping between bass player and soloist.

sections.label: A · Violin and flute in B minor
sections.mNote: Dotted phrases pass between the three soloists

sections.label: B · Flute refrain in F♯ minor
sections.mNote: The harpsichord answers the flute’s four-bar refrain

sections.label: C · G major, then the keyboard
sections.mNote: A varied refrain leads to the longest keyboard reply

sections.label: A′ · B minor, violin leading
sections.mNote: The violin brings back the opening phrase

cues.title: Three players remain
cues.text: The violin starts; the flute answers. Beneath their dotted phrases the harpsichord walks a bass line, then brings its right hand into the conversation. The accompanying strings have the whole movement off.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft full score (1871), II, pp. 149–151: flute, solo violin and harpsichord only. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ed/IMSLP02043-BWV1050.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A parcel for Brandenburg
cues.text: On 24 March 1721 Bach dates the dedication of six concertos to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg. Each concerto brings a different group of players: this one puts a flute beside a violin and a harpsichord.
cues.evidence: The dedication and the scoring are preserved in the 1721 presentation manuscript. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg_Concerto_No._5

cues.title: The flute in F♯ minor
cues.text: The little refrain reaches F♯ minor, with the flute leading and the violin answering. When the harpsichord takes over, its right hand keeps the dotted rhythm and decorates it; the left hand carries on underneath.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), II, p. 150: the third refrain and following keyboard episode.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: G major opens out
cues.text: The refrain turns to G major. The flute leads again, but Bach reshapes the phrase before handing it to the harpsichord. The keyboard’s reply is the longest in the movement, with flute and violin adding brief comments.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), II, pp. 150–151, fourth refrain and episode. The movement’s form is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg_Concerto_No._5.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bach with a violin
cues.text: In 1703, eighteen-year-old Bach spends about half a year playing violin in Duke Johann Ernst III’s private orchestra at Weimar. Later that year he takes the organist’s job in Arnstadt. The violin is part of his working life before the organ brings him a reputation.

cues.title: The violin brings it home
cues.text: The violin recovers the first phrase in B minor, and the flute answers as it did at the start. The harpsichord’s right-hand solo ends; its bass supports the last exchange and the closing chord.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), II, p. 151, final system: return of the opening refrain and B-minor cadence.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The flute takes F♯ minor
transitions.from: A · Violin and flute in B minor
transitions.to: B · Flute refrain in F♯ minor
transitions.how: The harpsichord’s running right-hand line finishes and the flute brings back the dotted refrain in F♯ minor. The violin answers it over the keyboard bass. Bach marks the returning solo lines forte; the harpsichord returns to accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), II, p. 150, first and second systems: third refrain.

transitions.title: The refrain turns to G major
transitions.from: B · Flute refrain in F♯ minor
transitions.to: C · G major, then the keyboard
transitions.how: The flute and violin reclaim the dotted phrase in G major, marked forte, while the keyboard supplies the bass. This refrain varies the opening melody. Its close releases another right-hand harpsichord solo, with the other two players answering in short phrases.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), II, pp. 150–151: fourth refrain and final keyboard episode.

transitions.title: The violin restores B minor
transitions.from: C · G major, then the keyboard
transitions.how: The extended keyboard solo ends. Over the harpsichord’s bass, the violin starts the opening B-minor refrain and the flute answers. Both solo lines are marked forte; the keyboard’s right hand withdraws into accompaniment for the final cadence.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1871), II, p. 151, final system.

source.title: Bach, Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, BWV 1050 — Bach-Gesellschaft full score (1871)
source.locator: II. Affettuoso, printed pp. 149–151: flute, solo violin and harpsichord alone. The dotted refrain passes through B minor, F♯ minor and G major before returning home.

timeline.note: Violin and flute exchange a dotted phrase over the harpsichord’s bass. The keyboard answers between their statements.
The flute begins the refrain in F♯ minor. The harpsichord answers with its written-out upper part.
The refrain reaches G major, followed by the longest keyboard reply. Violin and flute interrupt with their dotted phrase.
Violin and flute restore the opening exchange in B minor. The harpsichord accompanies them to the close.

composer.epithet: He supplied Leipzig’s churches with music for twenty-seven years and left keyboard players enough work for a lifetime.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education.

In 1703 Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and married his second cousin Maria Barbara. His cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, already makes two people say different things together: one sings the psalmist’s plea, another a hymn in long notes above it.
